newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Low spreads, drought hit Sri Lanka banks in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Low spreads, drought hit Sri Lanka banks in 1996.

text.p: The performance of Sri Lankan banks and financial institutions was badly hit in 1996 by low spreads as a result of increased competition and poor economic growth due to a crippling drought, analysts said on Friday.

"The commercial banks were affected by both factors while the development finance institutions were mostly affected by drought related problems," said Channa Kurukulasuriya, head of research at brokerage Lanka Securities.

Net profits of the four listed commercial banks Hatton National Bank Ltd, Commercial Bank Ld, Sampath Bank Ltd, Seylan Bank Ltd grew by only an average two percent last year compared to 15 percent in the previous five years, he said.

The four listed commercial banks and two development finance institutions -- Development Finance Corp of Ceylon Ltd and National Development Bank Ltd -- form the bulk of Sri Lanka's banking and finance sector stocks listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange.
"The two development banks were hit by depressed economic conditions which did not warrant expansions, and a lack of capital gains due to poor stock market performance in 1996," said Kurukulasuriya.
Low spreads were prompted by two new banks launching operations in 1996, bankers said. Sri Lanka now has 26 commercial banks, of which eight are local and 18 foreign.

"New banks had to offer higher deposit rates to get new business, forcing old ones to trim spreads just to keep customers," said Mangala Boyagoda, treasury manager of Union Bank, one of the new banks.

The new banks are paying about 15 percent on deposits and lending at about 20. This has forced older banks, which were taking deposits at an average rate of 11 percent and lending at about 22 percent, to cut spreads, analysts said.

Last year's drought brought average daily power cuts of five hours between March and August. This hit industrial production and led to a drop in capital requirement as corporate expansions were put on hold.

"About 100 million rupees of interest income had to be postponed last year because facilities had to be restructured due to the poor economic environment," said Rienzie Wijetilleke, chief executive of Hatton National Bank, whose profits were down six percent to 452.6 million rupees last year.
Analysts, however, forecast average profit growth of about five percent in 1997 for the four listed banks, but said they will have to face up to spreads which will continue to shrink.

"Business will improve if the economy improves. But efficiency will have to increase because margins will continue to be squeezed as the Central Bank has shown it is determined to keep rates low with the recent relaxation in monetary policy," said Savanthi Arthenayake, banking sector analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming.
The Central Bank cut the reserve ratios of commercial banks by one percent to 14 percent in January, and allowed exporters to borrow foreign currency locally to improve rupee liquidity.
It has said that the economic conditions are likely to improve this year, and the gross domestic product growth is expected to be over 5.5 percent against an estimated four percent in 1996.
